review:
For people who don't know what this game includes, It is a Trilogy game which includes:

1- Deponia, (main Game).

2- Chaos on Deponia.

3- Goodbye Deponia.

Because they were so lazy to add this in the Key Features section for some reason

NOTE:
"Deponia: The Complete Journey" is a bundle containing the first three Deponia games plus extra material (developer commentary etc).

This means that with this purchase you get these three games:
1) Deponia
2) Chaos on Deponia
3) Goodbye Deponia

This purchase does, however, NOT contain the 4th part of the Deponia saga, "Deponia Doomsday".
As of writing this (October 2020) there is no Deponia 5.

For some reason the description does not explain any of this. Bad form by the publishers!

Oh, and the game is fun! :-)

What I feel is essentially a love letter to the Point-and-Click adventures many of us grew up on, this game carries the same endearing cartoonish art, situational humor, and click-on-everything-you-see-until-something-happens gameplay that we've missed since we were kids. This game brought back the kind of magic and wonder and bemusement I haven't felt in ages, with a more mature dialogue that's more palatable for me as an adult.

Seriously, I usually fill my reviews with jokes and sarcasm, but this I'm serious about. This game is worth a try, I recommend it to everyone, period, no matter what kind of games you're into.

[h2]Weird German point-and-click adventure made by weirdos for weirdos[/h2]

A very weird German-made game. It's a point-n-click game centered around off-ball humour. The main protagonist is a irreverent, self-centered, egotiscal scumbag. Most of the humour, game mechanics and story beats play off Rufus' lack of self-awareness and supporting cast roasting him.

The collection comes with 3 games (Deponia, Chaos on Deponia & Goodbye Deponia). For the money, you get a fair amount of playtime (easily 40+ hrs). Only real negative is the inclusion of some tough puzzles that defy regular logic. If that doesn't put you off, I would strongly recommend this series.

Deponia: The Complete Journey contains the first three Deponia Games (Deponia, Chaos on Deponia, and Goodbye Deponia) it is NOT a separate game.  I made the mistake of thinking it was a separate individual game on it own and ended up buying all three original games PLUS The Complete Journey but luckily it was during one of STEAM's massive sales and they were all super cheap.  The good thing is that it gave me a chance to compare all three games with this collection.

Since this is a collection of the first 3 games, if you actually have any of those 3 games you are probably better off just buying the other 2 individually unless you find the collection is on sale and offer a better price then it would cost to buy the other 2 games (which does happen).  If you don't have any of them I would say just buy this collection.  For the most part, there isn't anything really different between the game play on the collection vs the game play in the individual games.  Graphics are the same, sound is the same.  The biggest difference is that this collection offers "director's commentary" in the game.  The bard who sings the opening, cut-scene, and end scene parts is the in-game avatar for the Games director (I want to say Pokki is his name but it's been a while and now I'm neither sure of the spelling or the name itself).  With the director's commentary you see a circle in the upper corner with his image.  Every scene you are in (including mini-games... which he loves by-the-way) has that circle.  

You click on the circle and you can hear commentary about the game related to that scene.  Some of it is background on making the game, design, sounds, dialogue, etc... but occasionally it actually gives away hints as to how to complete something in that area.  Since it does occasionally give spoilers I'd recommend playing through the game at least once without listening to the commentary but if you're really stuck it might also be beneficial to listen to it since it could help you move forward.  Not every scene has spoilers in the commentary though.  I found the commentary to be funny and entertaining.  I had already played through the games (the individual versions with no commentary) so the spoilers were not an issue for me.  My biggest disappointment with this collection is that it feels like there should be an achievement for having listened to all the commentary but unfortunately there is not.

The only real difference is that some of the achievements.  In the individual games Almost all the achievements are available except Droggeljug from Deponia (1).  However, Deponia: The Complete Journey offers three additional achievements not available in the individual games: Story Time (Goodbye Deponia), Journey Completed (upon completing all three games), Junkyard King (Deponia (1)).  Also the droggeljug mode from Deponia (1) which is available only after playing the game through at least once, is not available (which is obviously why the achievement cannot be obtained either).

Since that pretty much sums up all the essential differences in this collection compared to the individual games the rest of this will be review of the individual games:

[u][b] DEPONIA [/b][/u]
Deponia is the first game in the series.  I had heard many people say it was a good game especially for those like me who grew up on classic Point & Click adventures like King's Quest and Monkey Island.  To be honest the whole garbage/junkyard planet theme made it seem quite unappealing to me.  I'm not really into post apocalyptic dystopian future type stuff so for a long time I just ignored this game.  After having played it I wish I had looked past that a long time ago and picked the game up sooner.  It really is a great game.  It is a point and click adventure game and it's really fun.  It's got great graphics, great characters, great audio, great voice-over quality, etc... I have very few complaints about the game.  My only real complaint is the inventory system which is sometimes difficult.  It's supposed to be on screen and you can click it to open the inventory but sometimes it randomly disappears.  If that happens you have to push "i" and it will still drop down.  Besides that though I find it randomly has trouble selecting the inventory item or drops it as your trying to use it which means you sometimes have to attempt to grab and use an inventory item several times before you can actually use it.

In this Game our Main character Rufus is leaving his ex-girlfriends home (he's been living there with her for quite some time simply mooching off of her) and he's planning on traveling to Elysium which is a utopia in the sky.  He builds himself a device to transport himself there but on his journey instead finds a damsel-in distress (Goal) who he falls in love with and tries to save accidentally getting them both dumped off the cruiser to Elysium and right back where he started but now he has to try and wake her up and then get both of them to Elysium.  Rufus... is a sort of anti-hero.  He's a real jerk who generally thinks only of himself.  He's the kind of person you hate to deal with in real life but he's a sort of lovable Jerk so he's a lot of fun to play in a game.

[u][b] CHAOS ON DEPONIA [/b][/u]
Chaos on Deponia is the Sequel to Deponia and picks up with Goal trying to warn Elysium that there are still people living on Deponia and Rufus is still hell-bent on getting himself to Elysium (and also reuniting with Goal).  Of course he mucks it up and causes problems.  Now he's damaged Goals implant and has to try and fix it... he makes it worse and now he's got to convince three Goal personalities to work with/like him while still working towards fixing her overall damaged implant.  I personally didn't really care for the 3-way split personality and having to change between them but the game is fun enough that it's not a huge drawback.  You get to explore new places in this game and meet new characters (including someone else very important to Rufuf's life who I won't give away here and spoil).  There's some fun references in the game like Cuthulu and there's A LOT of platypuses... or is it platypi?  Some parts of the game feel a little tedious having to walk back and forth for one thing but it's not too bad.  The inventory issue I mentioned in the previous game is still a problem though.

[u][b] GOODBYE DEPONIA [/b][/u]
Goodbye Deponia is the third (supposedly at the time, final conclusion) game of the series.  Rufus is still trying to get to Elysium and Goal is still trying to warn them that people are still on the surface.  People who like/help Rufus the most are starting to tire of him a little too much, his relationship with Goal is stronger but strained and he's struggling with being the good self-sacrificing guy vs. his usual jerk he is.  In this game we get a lot more background filled in to finally learn why he and Cletus look so similar and there are some emotional roller coasters game-wise too.  Many of the characters from previous games continue to pop-up in this third installment too.  Inventory is still problematic.

'Deponia: The Complete Journey' is a point-and-click adventure game compilation that consists of the first three games of the series: 'Deponia', 'Chaos on Deponia', and 'Goodbye Deponia'. Together, they tell the story of Rufus' quest to leave garbage-filled surface of Deponia for the idyllic floating town of Elysium.

'D:TCJ' is the best way to experience the grand scope and epic nature of Rufus' journey. The pacing of each of the three games is somewhat uneven, with overly long middle sections that seem to go nowhere. Thankfully, it is in these middle sections that we find the more interesting puzzles and fun mini games, which help you stay motivated. All three games, when played back to back in 'D:TCJ', present a clearer story and character arcs.

One of the most captivating aspects of 'D:TCJ' is the beautifully drawn characters and locales. The appealing art design, and the detail with which the characters and locations are realized, give the recent Remastered releases of LucasArts games a run for their money. The trash-covered planet of Deponia is an imaginative and visually stunning one, which was surprising to me at first given that it is covered with garbage. However, Deponia is a lot more lively and vibrant than one would imagine.

The English voice acting in 'D:TCJ' is also spot-on, adding personality to the interesting characters. Rufus is particularly unique among adventure game heroes. Whereas main characters of popular adventure games can be heroic, quirky, clumsy, or perhaps have their share of foibles, Rufus is just not (very) likeable and not even an anti-hero at all, for he is egotistic, narcissistic, and self-centred. And yet, he is captivating as a playable character, in part due to the great voice acting by Kerry Shales. Even when reasons for Rufus' faults are revealed and explained, it feels abrupt and a bit like damage control. You will definitely find divisive opinions on whether or not Rufus is a good main character in an adventure game.

You will also find divisive opinions on the jokes in 'D:TCJ'. Some people find them funny, some not. Personally, I find the game amusing -- not very funny, but entertaining enough. This could be due to the funny bits being lost in translation from the original German (and the game is very self-aware of it), or it could be simply due to what people find funny. However, I did find some scenarios, jokes and characters depiction off-putting, sexist, and culturally insensitive. Whether or not you can overlook these flaws is up to you.

However, I can definitively say that the puzzles in this game are fun. Some are challenging, some require some form of moon logic, and some tickle your brain just enough. Despite the length of the game (I easily clocked in over 24 hours of gaming time in total despite what my stats say because I played parts of the game offline), there is a good variety of puzzles to keep gameplay fresh. The art and the puzzles are definitely highlights of 'D:TCJ', and I very much enjoyed the game in spite of the flaws I previously mentioned.

'D:TCJ' is a great adventure game. It embodies both strengths and weaknesses of great adventure games that came before. Questionable quality of jokes and content aside, it definitely deserves the accolades that it received. It is a must-play for anyone who enjoys point-and-click adventure games.

P.S.: For achievement seekers like I, you will find some achievements for 'D:TCJ' very difficult to get, let alone figure out what they are about. mishalunchbox wrote fantastic walkthroughs and [URL=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=875459798]achievement guides[/URL] that you should definitely consult if you are interested in getting all achievements.

Is this game a masterpiece? It would be, IF... Deponia: The Complete Story is the magnus opus of Daedalic - a company often referred to as LucasArts successor (until they left the adventure genre, like their role model). This edition consists of the first three parts of the series, and it took me around 50 hours to finish it. I obviously enjoyed it, because the game offers well-structured puzzles, fantastic 2D visuals, professional voice-overs and a polished engine. The main parts of each of the three games take place in just one, quite large location. In Deponia you spend most of your time in your hometown with around 25 single screens, all full of hotspots, items, characters and often connected in some way. Chaos in Deponia takes place mostly in the Floating Black Market (and then on the surrounding isles), which is even a bit larger, while in the final part you are split into three separate characters exploring (most of the time) three separate parts of Porta Fisco - switching items between them. Puzzles are solved by using items, talking to characters, and the game contains various minigames. You can never die, you can never reach a dead-end, the story is kind of... funny. There are a lot of missable cheavos - I just got  67 of 105. The whole thing would be perfect.

It is not, though. You might dislike your character, Rufus, who is an annoying moron. But, well, you cannot always play the perfect hero. There are a bunch of other charming characters during the game as well, some in all three parts, some have to endure Rufus only for a shorter time. I personally loved his ex-girlfriend Toni. The story, while funny, has a bunch of twists that may not really make sense, but we are used to that from (not only) adventure games. More importantly, the game always kind of tells you what needs to be done next and drops a lot of hints on how to get there. Really well-done.

There is one thing that cannot be ignored, though: The Complete Edition contains at least two game-breaking bugs (and a bunch of other not game-breaking bugs). Two of the minigames in Deponia simply cannot be finished, which might not even be too obvious. So you are stuck, and don't even realize that you are stuck. I could only get past this by downloading a saved game from the (still working) homepage. The bugs are well-documented, but Daedalic is obviously not able to fix them. I am only upvoting the game because the rest of the game is really, really good. 

[u][b] Conclusion:[/b][/u]
Near-perfect, long adventure in a cartoon universe - with two broken, game-stopping minigames in the first part.

I have purchased all of the individual games as well as this complete journey set because this is one the the most entertainingly fun point and click puzzle adventures I have ever been on.  With an adult-like story line focused on an egotistical main character you are plunged head first into the life of a Deponian.  Your main character, Rufus, wants what any normal adult wants...the life of ease and comfort.  

I recommend this game to any adventurer with an avid love for decent puzzles and great plot.  
Happy Gaming!

This is a game about Rufus. And how awesome Rufus is. And his heroism. And how he always gets the girl. And how Rufus DOESN'T spend most of the game running around clicking on things, strapping himself to giant sawblades, getting his teeth knocked out, annoying the hell out of his sadistic ex-girlfriend, accidentally giving away his family heirlooms, polluting the water supply, practicing necromancy on fish, sawing Goal's personality into three parts for a lollipop, making weird faces, and other things that a hero clearly would never do. 

Because Rufus is a true hero. This is a game about heroism. He didn't do ANYTHING mentioned above, and this certainly isn't an entire game trilogy about him doing those things.

The complete anthology of Rufus' adventures to save the world.
I repeat - all parts in one. This is not a sequel - not a spinoff, nor a separate story - these are the same games, but instead of separate games, they are included in one.
Why am I focusing on this? Everything is simple.
Having all parts of Deponia in my library, I also saw Deponia: The Complete Journey at the sale. And since the game is very fun, with its own unique world and characters - I thought it was a continuation of the series and... of course I bought it.
So, I got a copy of the games I already have in my library.
However, I recommend this game to buy and get acquainted with the world of Deponia - for those who somehow missed this series in their gaming life. And also for those who do NOT have original parts in stock.

To try to convince my mother to get this game, I described it as "Monkey Island for the Modern Era". 

I actually feel this game fits in with the humour style from the first 4 Monkey Island games better than the Telltale series does. 

It's truly a great game IMO and anyone who enjoyed Monkey Island (especially games 2 and 3) will enjoy this.

My recommendation comes with a reservation for those on the fence.

The artwork, story, music, gameplay, comedy and Deponia mythology are all top shelf. In fact it's so well-done I found myself occasionally feeling like the puzzles were a hindrance to the story. If puzzle solving is your primary interest then don't hesitate to buy these games, you should be very satisfied. If you ever feel like puzzles can be a nuisance then do NOT buy these games. If you're somewhere in the middle then buy the games and follow a guide whenever you feel like the pace has become stagnant.

Besides pace I have two more critiques: it doesn't mention in-game you can double click destination arrows to insta-travel. I played for nearly an hour before discovering this. Achievement hunters take note: for better or worse (it's worse) this package bundles all 105 achieves across the 3 games into one set. So you're committed to ~30 hours of gameplay to get to 100%, and that will be for 1 perfect game not three.

Overall I got more than a bargain for my $8 and would love more Deponia story/mythology, but perhaps in another format.

I only bought this game because of pretty redhead girl and nice discount. I didn't expect much, not from a point and click  game. And I certainly didn't expect great humour, challenging puzzles or amazing story. And the feelings...this game moved the feelings inside me that I thought were already dead. Simply amazing.

Not Recommended

I really wanted to enjoy this game, but there’s a critical bug that completely blocks progression, and it’s still not fixed after more than a year. The issue appears during a mandatory mini-game and makes it impossible to continue the story. Dozens of players have reported it, yet the developers haven’t provided a working patch or workaround.

I can’t recommend a game that leaves you stuck with no way to finish it. Until the developers actually fix this long-standing game-breaking bug, save your money and your time.

A really good game with a fun story. 

You're put in the role of Rufus who tries to escape the trash-planet Deponia. Rufus is reckless, egoistical and prone to injury. In general a bad person. He'd literally sell a person into slavery for 5c and has no problem feeding orphans to slime-monsters. But here we are, the worst person on the planet trying to save the planet. 

Puzzles seem a bit un-intuitive at times and even looking up solutions didn't always tell me how I was supposed to figure it out on my own, but except for one or two I sincerely enjoyed them. 

Characters and humor are amazing. Having to stick with Rufus bad decisions sometimes feels painfully forced, but seeing the hilarious fails that come as a result totally makes up for it. 

Even with a little help from the interwebs, it took me almost 23 hours to complete the entire journey. Since I got it on sale, it was more than worth its price, but I think even the regular price is reasonable and fair. I had my fair share of laughs. 10/10 would buy again.

This is one of the best, if not the best, point-and-click (P&C) 2D adventure game of this decade. A must-play for adventure gamers out there (although, if you are an avid adventure gamer, you probably would have played this title long before I reviewed this). You can check out the amount of awards won by this game listed on this STEAM page. 

[b] FYI, "Deponia: The Complete Journey" consist of 3 games combined into 1 complete package: [/b]
1. Deponia (released in January 2012)
2. Chaos on Deponia (released in November 2012)
3. Goodbye Deponia (released in October 2012)

[h1] PROS: [/h1]
+ Amazing 2D graphic. Sharp, detail and simply beautiful (check out the screenshots for yourself!)
+ Very high production value
+ Good, lengthy story for each of the 3 games
+ Some really funny jokes 
+ Very good plot / adventure
+ Sound, cut-scene videos and music are high quality
+ Top notch animation

[h1] CONS: [/h1]
- Unless you are a hardcore P&C adventure gamer, this game cannot be played without a walkthrough. Some of the puzzles are absurd (for the sake of being funny) and cannot be solved without a proper guide. 
- The game is originally in German, but now available in many different languages. Even though the English translation is very well done, once in a while, the jokes or sentences will feel or sound a little strange (due to inter-language adaptation. meaning it sounds perfectly normal/funny in German, but less funny in English)
- I honestly can't think of anything else.

With 41.8 hours on record, I just finished "Deponia:  The Complete Journey" with 100% Achievements.  I would have probably taken a tad longer, but I had played the first game in this compendium ("Deponia") stand-alone somewhat earlier (so you can probably add eight or nine hours to my expected play).  As with the stand-alone version, I'm recommending this version (which, along with "Deponia," includes "Chaos on Deponia" and "Goodby Deponia).  The game play across all three games is pretty consistent:  a pretty good point-and-click game with very good art work, tongue-in-cheek humor, and good voice-acting.  The puzzle difficulty does vary across the games just a bit (I'd say the second game is a bit easier than the first, and the third game harder than the first two).  I've got three gripes with the game.  First, the protagonist, Rufus is a jerk.  If there were more character growth in him as the game progressed, I'd have been happier.  But, it's just sort of irritating to have him constantly do really wrong things at every turn for three games (he actually gets worse from game to game).  Second, as I mentioned, the third game is harder than the first two.  Unfortunately, it's hard enough that I had to resort to walk-throughs a lot (a LOT).  I don't mind getting stuck a couple of times in a game, but in the third game I was stuck most of the time.  And finally, I'm not very happy with the penultimate ending:  it's possible I'm interpreting it wrong, but it's pretty mean even with the one alternative interpretation I can come up with.  Even with those complaints, the game is still well-worth the price and time.

This is a set of the first three out of a four-game "quadrilogy" of point-and-click adventure games. They have silly but fun stories, a few memorable characters, some nice puzzles, and...some perplexing puzzles that mar the experience a bit. Over all, it's a good time and I do recommend these games, but don't expect to beat them without having to reference a walkthrough several times. I grew up playing point-and-click adventure games, yet I still had to look up solutions quite a bit, especially in the third game, "Goodbye Deponia."

If you're interested, Deponia Doomsday is the fourth game, which is not contained in this pack. I really liked it as well, and would recommend it too, though you'll probably want to make sure you like the first three games, contained in this pack, before buying the fourth.

To start of with the good things, the art in the game is beautiful and full of details, the music and voice acting are also very good and despite what I'm going to say further in the review the game has its funny moments.

Now to why I don't recommend this game, It's a point & click adventure game, therefore its gameplay is based on solving puzzles, mini-games and talking to people, It would be very good if the puzzles made sense at least 50% of the time, but they don't, you are forced to waste in a seemingly endless process of trial and error and frustration.

Another problem is the relationship between the main character(Rufus) and his love interest(goal), see the thing is, they don't have enough interaction to actually have a believable romantic relationship, goal spends most of her time incapacitated, [spoiler] brain damaged, split into three personalities, dead or as a child, all of which were cause by Rufus	 [/spoiler].Refuse's personality is also a problem, at first you think he is goofy and misunderstood and you actually like him, but then he keeps screwing up and doing despicable things, as you progress in the game you notice that he's just incredibly selfish, he only wants to save the world so to that people will call him a hero, he deliberately destroys peoples lives and put them in danger to get his way, in time you start to dislike Rufus and his relationship with Goal becomes incredibly unbelievable.

I normally love dark humor, but sometimes even humor has limits, killing baby dolphins and turning them into cat food made me cringe but I let that pass, as I let a lot of other things pass,his sexism for example, now when Rufus sells the only black woman in the game into slavery and then makes her dress and dance as a monkey, yeah a monkey, before he did that almost delivered 4 children to a pedophile [spoiler] child Goal included [/spoiler] then proceeds to masturbate said pedophile with a inked paper and shows the did*k imprint to the 4 children, doing that made me fell disgusted, the game gives you no choice to avoid that, unless of course you quit and uninstal the game.

This edition of Deponia series is so infested in bugs that it is literally unplayable. I was stuck in the first chapter of the first game in two different spots (for the knowledgeable: the explosion puzzle and the pidgeon puzzle) and decided I do not want to risk getting softlocked later in the game.
I have also noticed that the developers were refusing to fix these bugs even back in 2017, which is, frankly, unacceptable.

Another thing: the newly added Hint system is both useless (does not update properly with the progress AND does not give you hints, shockingly) and annoying (instead, gives you insufferable "DING" sound every time you correctly do anything) and cannot be turned off.

Whoever stumbles on this review: the trilogy IS good, it IS worth your time, but NOT in the "Complete Journey" format. Buy individual games.

I played the original Deponia games years ago now, and recently decided to replay the series through this. In theory, it’s great, but as it stands right now, I don’t think this version is worth buying or playing.

This game is over 10 years old, and is currently being sold for £25.99. That might seem pretty decent for three great point & click games, but given that this complete package version is riddled with bugs and seems all but abandoned, it’s worth reconsidering.
I went into this blind, and found out quite quickly that this game has a lot of issues. I hit a game-breaking bug in the first chapter of the first game. The discussions page is full of people asking questions about game-breaking & achievement blocking bugs that date all the way back to 2016. The bugs haven’t been addressed, and as far as I could see the developers haven’t commented in the discussions page for this version in a long while.
I did, however, find that the page for the singular version of game 1: Deponia had a developer write a comment in the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/214340/discussions/0/846961716447233058/?ctp=9]discussions[/url] fairly recently claiming they are going to update all Deponia games at some point to address bugs they have long known about. Giving that they are releasing a new game "Surviving Deponia" with an ETA of 2025, I think it's fair to assume this is true. It is not clear though if these updates will include The Complete Journey or if this only applies to the separate copies.
I’m sure the separate games have bugs also, but from looking at the discussion pages between them all, for now it seems like the separate copies are the more stable choice, with the biggest chance of being fixed in future.

In terms of the games, I will give an overview here of my opinion, but I have written more detailed reviews on each of the games separately.

As far as point & click adventure games go, these are on the classic side of things. You steal everything around you, use and combine items to solve puzzles and further the story. There is a moderate amount of dialogue, and there isn’t a lot of hand-holding.

The story for me feels as though the developers weren’t taking things all that seriously and was kind of making things up as they went along. Given that this franchise has a bit of a goofy humorous vibe to it, I don’t think that this is a bad thing. At all times you know what the overall plan is, but there are a lot of twists and turns that make the details of the story chaotic and difficult to follow as well as the lesson of the story rarely being brought to the forefront. I think these games prioritise fun, and there being twists, over there being a cohesive watertight narrative.
A lot of people were disappointed in the ending to this original trilogy back when it first came out, so much so that the developers came out with "Deponia Doomsday", which I’ve heard is an “alternative ending” type of game. 
Personally, I actually enjoyed how these games ended. When the game is such chaos, the one thing you had to fall back on was what the game had repeated, non-stop, the plan was. Then, when the game ends differently to what people may have thought, they were left with a sour, disappointed taste in their mouth. Because it was put so into focus, how could it have ended any differently?
Although unexpected, I enjoyed it and felt that it was a fitting end if you thought about what point the game might be trying to make.

The art, animation, music, voice-acting and humour overall are great. You notice a jump up in quality from Deponia 1 to 2, and the series always felt like it was improving itself in some way or another.

Puzzle wise, these games need your attention. I don't think you can play them casually, as they often have moments of opening up, so you have multiple areas with multiple puzzles all to solve at once. Examining everything, paying attention and keeping notes on things you haven’t solved or interacted with in an area are all advised.
Between "Entirely logical" and "Completely nonsensical", I would say the point & click puzzles here sit somewhere in the middle. For the most part they are logical, but every now and then there is the odd puzzle you need to think outside of the box for. I think getting stuck and resorting to a guide at some point or another is pretty much guaranteed with this series.

Achievements wise, this series has a [b]lot[/b] of missable achievements. This version also has some achievement-blocking bugs. It can be done, but there are some tedious ones as it is, so also working around bugs may prove to be frustrating.

Overall, I loved these games when I first played them and I still enjoyed it this time through. I think any point & click fan would enjoy these, and despite the ending being disliked by some, I stand by it and think it was an appropriate way to end the series.
I hope the fixes come soon, either on this or the separate versions, as at this point I see these as modern classics.

It’s got all the charm of old point & click adventure games—the characters are weird and irreverent, the puzzles are obtuse in a way that can make them funny, the art and animations are immersive, and the areas you visit are scenic and full of character. It's great to see a relatively modern (as in, within the past 10 years) adventure game carrying on the legacy of the genre.

Unfortunately, it goes too far in some of those places. As many other people complain, the main character is often just annoying. You have to learn early on not to try to relate to him or be concerned for him, because he ruins everything for everyone around him. Rufus is like a force of nature, and you have to treat him that way. Don’t pray that he “does the right thing this time”—he’s capricious and unpredictable. Just enjoy the spectacle from afar. Even then, though, he can be REALLY annoying.

In a similar vein, it’s annoying how the plot can be artificially drawn out by Rufus’s shenanigans. Especially in the third game, certain long puzzle segments only exist because of problems Rufus created himself. It messes with the flow of the game; you’re interested in finding out where the story is going, but then you have to spend an hour on busywork to fix something that was working just fine until Rufus broke it.

Some of the puzzle solutions are funny, but the sense of “oh come on what am I supposed to do” can rob you of the enjoyment. I highly recommend using a guide when you get stuck for more than 10 minutes, unless you’re really committed to having the classic adventure game experience. The story, characters, and the environments are good parts of the game that are still fully enjoyable without spending hours being stuck because you couldn’t figure out you had to combine two silly items together. Considering this is three games in one, you’ll likely appreciate the faster pace that a guide brings, so that you aren’t spending 100 hours on this trilogy.

Still, as long as you don't let the puzzles wear you out and upset you (by using a guide when you've tried everything you can think of), and you don't try to use Rufus as a self-insert character, the good outweighs the bad. The writing, while off in places (like anything regarding Goal's attitude toward Rufus), is fun and well-paced. The English voice acting is fantastic, which is surprising given that the developers are German, and the art style, animations, cutscenes, and locales are great. Make no mistake though—while the story is fun, it's not necessarily [i]good[/i]. It's mostly intentionally silly, which makes some of the serious scenes fail to elicit any response from the reader; especially when Rufus ruins them.

Note: if you run the game at a refresh rate above 60 Hz (like if you have a 144 Hz monitor), you’ll have trouble clicking items in your inventory—most of your clicks won’t register, and you’ll have to click 2+ times to select an item. You can fix this by setting your monitor’s refresh rate to 60 Hz. This problem is fixed in the fourth game, Deponia Doomsday.

A must play for point and click adventure fans! This is a truly unique experience that has aged remarkably well. The characters are memorable, the voice acting is strong, and the world is imaginative and full of variety. The puzzles are often innovative, creative, and thoughtfully designed, frequently encouraging out of the box thinking. The game also does a good job of providing fair hints to gently guide the player forward. One of its biggest strengths is the sheer amount of dialogue even in places where most developers would cut corners. It’s clear the creators put genuine care and effort into making this a complete and polished experience. The humor is generally excellent, though it can occasionally cross into edgy or bad-taste territory, which may not sit well with everyone.

The main drawback is puzzle difficulty. While most are clever, a few are extremely hard and rely on repeating actions or very specific positioning to trigger unexpected results. One such moment was brilliant, while another felt firmly in “moon logic” territory. When you genuinely feel stuck and the in game guide offers no help, it’s best to briefly consult a walkthrough preferably a video guide, as some solutions must be done in a precise order and text guides can accidentally spoil other puzzles. I only needed outside help a handful of times, which isn’t bad considering this is a lengthy, puzzle heavy trilogy. Patience, taking breaks, and approaching problems from different angles are key. I also encountered a few minor bugs that caused progress issues, so saving often is highly recommended. Overall, a fantastic adventure that rewards persistence and curiosity.

The Deponia series is a classic point-and-click adventure where you control Rufus, a young man living on the planet of Deponia, and trying to get to the idylic floating city of Elysium. 

As far as point-and-clicks go, Deponia is pretty-much what you'd expect. You talk to characters to learn about the story and figure out what you need to do to progress, as well as pick-up, combine, and use items to solve problems. The series also features mini-games, though if that isn't your thing or you just get frustrated with them, there is the Skip option which auto-solves them for you so you can continue. 

Design-wise the game looks great, with its animated style. The characters are quirky and interesting, and the voice-acting is good as well. It's a funny game that had me laughing out loud more than once. There were a few occasions where the solutions for puzzles were a bit out of left-field, but they are, for the most part, fairly solid. The only actual gameplay issue I had was the fact that, for some reason, it didn't always like to let me select items in my inventory. For whatever reason, I would sometimes need to click an item multiple times to select it. Thankfully, that was only an issue for the earlier parts of the series. 

Here's the basic premise of the story:
Deponia is a planet whose inhabitants generated so much garbage over time that the world is literally covered in it. Things are so bad for Deponia that finding clean water is like striking oil or discovering a gold mine. At some point in Deponia's history, the upper-crust elite built Elysium for themselves, an idylic city floating way above the trash-heaps, and conected to Deponia only by a single tether, which is guarded and patrolled by their military servants known as the Organon. Rufus, a citizen of Deponia, has long dreamed of escaping their garbage-heap of a planet and living in the lap of luxury in Elysium. Unfortunately for him, and everyone around him, Rufus, while remarkably clever in his own crazy way, is too lazy and conceited to bother with such things like considering the potential consequences of his actions or myriad ways in which his inane schemes could go wrong. As a result, he's known as a walking disaster, and is a social pariah. (Not that his ego would let him consider that he's anything but the greatest person on Deponia.) Things, however, take a different turn when Rufus comes across an Elysian woman named Goal, and realizes that helping her return to Elysium may be his own ticket in. Thus begins his adventure.

One of the more interesting things about Deponia is Rufus himself. Unlike most "heroes" he is only tolerated at best, and with good reason. He's careless, egotistical, and his main motivation is "how will this help ME?" This fact is often lampshaded by his friends as they groan in exasperation and wonder what spectacular way he'll screw things up this time. However, as terrible as Rufus can be, it also helps to highlight his good points. He may be an egotistical, self-serving jerkass, but that doesn't mean he doesn't care. In fact, there are several points where his zany schemes may actually have worked out if he hadn't sabotaged them himself to save his friends. (Of course, they wouldn't have been in danger if not for him, but still...) Rufus is a flawed character, a BADLY flawed character, but one can't help but root for him in the end. 

The rest of the other characters, both major and minor, play pretty well off the ego-centric Rufus, and the overall story and progression of the games is interesting, exciting, and amusing. If you're looking for a wacky point-and-click adventure that's laugh-out-loud funny, intriguing, and more than a little insane, I'd highly recommend Deponia.

Despite moments of brilliance and enough minigames to impress a Hasbro executive, there are a few critical problems with Deponia that are never addressed. As you may know, you're buying three games here. The first and especially the last are by far the strongest in terms of story and puzzles, while the second (middle) entry is fairly weak. It's going to sound like I'm being very hard on the game, but I actually like it quite a bit. It just has some core problems in writing and game design that are never addressed, even after 3 games. I'll be talking about story flaws and game design, but it will be worded in such a way that spoilers are avoided. 

The first problem is the story. The conceit of the adventure, the end goal that’s always hanging over Rufus’ head… it doesn’t make any sense. The protagonist’s only motivation is to reach to a place called Elysium. It is literally a glowing castle floating over the planet. Everyone Rufus meets tells him this is an impossible and foolish task. We never, ever learn why people think it’s impossible to reach Elysium. 

This problem is especially prevalent in the first 1/3 of the game because we learn there are multiple places on the planet where an ordinary cable car connects the ground to Elysium. Allegedly, the problem is that you need “ascension codes.” This doesn’t matter, of course, because there’s no reason on Deponia why someone couldn’t just make a second cable car. Everyone tells Rufus his goal is impossible or even acts like Elysium is a myth when there are literally cables connecting Deponia to the massive glowing castle in the sky. There is no reason given why the lower ascension station shouldn’t be a thriving city, rather than an abandoned ruin. 

Things only get worse once we learn the Elysian’s motivations. This problem is only compounded when the secondary antagonist essentially kidnaps someone to take back to Elysium, even showing off his prisoner, when it has been established on numerous occasions that the tertiary antagonist and Big Bad don’t want any Elysians to know about Deponians for various reasons. It seemingly throws a big fat rusty wrench into everything the game has been trying to tell us because nothing about Elysium in the game all about reaching Elysium and dealing with Elysian politics makes any sense. 

Then there’s the puzzles.  In practice, there are only four puzzles (not counting the diverse and interesting minigames) in the whole Deponia series. The way they are presented is generally enjoyable. Rather than gatekeeping (layered fetch quests to open next area) most of Deponia’s puzzles push the story forward and have rippling consequences. That’s good, but it doesn’t excuse that the solutions typically are…
1.	Trick person into doing something
2.	Analyze and modify a Rube Goldberg machine 
3.	Talk to someone until they do something for you 
4.	Realize item won’t work until its combined with another item. Then place new item in the same place. 

These puzzles get complicated awfully quickly and don’t always make a lot of sense. For example, you’re trying to make a guy trip on a banana peel, but he doesn't slip on it correctly. So you go on an extremely lengthy and convoluted side mission to straighten a banana for no reason. The result is that nothing different happens with the banana, but a different cutscene plays. Rufus could have solved the puzzle on his own all along, but we just wasted 45 minutes doing a stupid side puzzle that has no echos on the story.  

Every puzzle has multiple, multiple steps because the protagonist, Rufus, is a blithering idiot. Rufus is so bad, the entire second part of the trilogy could be completely ignored if Rufus acted like an actual person instead of a one-note cartoon character. The problem then is that the events at the start of the second game create a butterfly effect that makes the events of the third game almost unrecognizable. 

Many puzzles also simply rely on repetition. It may seem you’re out of options until you do the same thing over and over and over. One part forces Rufus to knock on a door three times under specific conditions to proceed. If you didn’t know that, it would quickly seem you were out of options. 

It’s because of moments like the door puzzle and the banana puzzle that it appears the writers may have been overindulgent. Many, many times while playing this game I got up in the middle of a conversation to go to the bathroom and when I came back the characters were still talking; the dialogue box still hadn’t opened. Characters, especially the soothsayer, drone on and on without saying anything of comedic or character value. Yes, we get it.  Rufus is an egomaniac. 

Rufus’ dialogue, even with familiar characters, constantly has to remind us of his single character trait over and over and over again. This is acceptable in the first chapter because they try to show Rufus has grown at the start of the second chapter. But the entire second game is caused by the fact that Rufus hasn’t grown even a little bit. By the start of the third game, he’s as bad as he was at the very start of the first game in spite of everything he’s done over the past 10 hours. It’s absolutely maddening to watch character progression that consistently takes one step forward and three steps back.

Rufus constantly lies about lying. He won’t give a straight answer. Whenever he’s confronted and simply asked to explain his side of the story, the writers just have him uncontrollably babbling “but I’m the good guy!” without a single ounce of context every. single. time. this happens. It’s an entire game based around the idiot ball trope.

The Deponia Complete Journey is a point-and-click adventure in the style of the LucasArts games. Visually it looks really nice and the simple interface which exposes only one generic "Look" and one generic "Interact" commands works pretty well.

You play as Rufus, a guy living on a planet completely submerged in trash (Deponia). Rufus is obsessed with reaching the legendary city of Elysium which smiles at deponians from up high in the sky. He soon gets involved with a girl called Goal and from that the plot will develop into a huge race to save the world.

Positive things about this game:
- Visually pleasant
- Dev commentary somewhat interesting
- Simple usable interface, with nice touches like middle-mouse button to highlight all interactable objects
- Quite funny (in the beginning)
- There are a lot of minigames in the game (expecially in the first chapters, there are very few in Goodbye Deponia, the last serie of chapters), most of them are quite fun.

Negative things about this:
- Okay, what was funny the first 2 times, is not funny the other 27475323234852472372434723520392074238947 times.
- A lot of puzzles don't make any sense at all. You get them either by coincidence or exclusion. You have to constantly resort to trial and error combining items with interactables.
- The game does very often a terrible job at hinting at what is the next action to take. They have added a "Chapter Log" in the Complete Journey edition which is supposed to give you hints as to what to do next and on how to accomplish things but it's ludicrously useless. Example of log entry with related hint: "You need to put [nospoiler] to sleep" - hint: "Find something to make [nospoiler] sleep". OH THAT'S REALLY HELPFUL THANKS.
- A LOT of puzzles make sense only after you have solved them (by chance or by getting fed up and looking at a walkthrough).
- The game forces you to make decisions which as a player you actively do not want to make in a lot of crucial moments.
- The ending is a MASSIVE disappointment, after a huge buildup and many hours of gameplay you are rewarded with so little that your entire game experience feels _completely pointless_. If you have played Mass Effect 3, it's the exact same kind of questionable story choice: you have spent hours on this game buuuuut we don't really care we are just forcing you to take our very "art-sy" ending and if you don't like it that's your problem.

If the ending had not been so INCREDIBLY BAD, I would have recommended this game. Sadly, the wrap-up of the story is so terrible that it _completely_ ruined my enjoyment of the game. It's a fun journey, even if it's a very frustrating one at times, but when you reach the end you are clearly expecting certain things to happen... and they don't, at all. It's so bad that it does not even follow its own logic, it's pretty much as terrible as Mass Effect 3 from this perspective.

Shame really, but save your money and spare yourself from a colossal disappointment. You will actively feel robbed of the time you spent playing the game.

I'm a huge fan of Monkey Island, Myst, and Sam & Max, so I confess my guilt and confusion that Deponia flew entirely under my radar for a long time.

However, upon a friend's recommendation, once I sat down to play it, I didn't stop until I'd finished the entire trilogy.

The reasons why it absorbed me are easy to identify: Story, World, and Characters.

The Story is fairly standard at a glance. It's about a self-centered antihero who thinks he deserves a better lot in life who by the end begrudgingly helps to save the world he so desperately wants to get away from. But escalating complexities in each character's conflicting motivations leaves you never quite sure who to root for, or who even to trust. Ultimately, it's a story about how people learn to tolerate each other.

The World is perhaps even more compelling. On the surface, it appears to be a mix of steampunk, science fiction, post-apocalypse. The setting bounces between the garbage planet Deponia and the the floating utopia Elysium, and sets up a class struggle between them. But there's also a message about prejudice in the way it demonstrates the vibrancy and resilience of people who eke out a living among garbage, or the complacency that breeds in sterile environments.

The Characters, however, made this game entirely. I said that it was a story about how people learn to tolerate each other, and to clarify, it's a story about people, none of which are innocent of selfishness or short-sightedness. But most of all, it's about how we as the player can learn to tolerate our antihero protagonist. And conversely, antagonists who seemed to be cut-and-dry evil begin to show more nuance. Even the female lead and romantic interest, who seems to be the moral touchstone and voice of reason behaves in strange ways that contradict her character.

Ultimately its cartoon animation and colorful art belies its deeper adult themes, partly because the characters are wonderful and hilarious, and partly because you have to cope with all the things you've done to them.

[h1]Short version: 85%[/h1]
If you haven’t bought the Deponia trilogy, the Complete Journey is the best option to experience this famous, not so child-friendly, but in the end quite enjoyable adventure game about a very egotistical protagonist and his struggles to save and/or leave his home planet.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Deponia: The Complete Journey adds very little to those who already played the trilogy as separate games– it is nothing but a merged version of them. But it is excellent for those who are new to the world of Deponia or want to play the whole story without interruptions (if we don’t count the tutorials, since they were left in there for all three parts).

On the surface, the story is about the struggles of the protagonist, Rufus, and his plans to escape the titular Deponia planet, so he can join the upper society of Elysium. But, looking closer, it is more of a tale of a very egotistical man who uses everyone to his advantage; not because he is evil, but because he honestly thinks he is doing the best for everybody by trying to do the best for himself. The result is not only some slapstick gold, but also excellent dialogues and character synergy between Rufus, his newfound love (Goal from Elysium), and all the others who help them or try to stand in their way.
The characters and the dialogue are the strong points of Deponia, even though the plot suffers from a few problems. It tends to get sidetracked all the time, and as the games progress, the number of plot holes and abandoned story threads increase drastically.

As a point ‘n’ click game, it shows an interesting difficulty curve: it starts off mild, then ramps it up to almost early 90s levels, only to end in some poorly designed or medium level puzzles. This creates a mixed bag for the Complete Edition, but a good bag nonetheless.

I’ll start off by going into the negatives, because I like to end on a more positive note.
[u]Negatives[/u]
[b]Illogical puzzles[/b]… Now this one technically fits the context of the game, because the main character is a narcissistic madman. But it does cause some frustration, as several solutions feel more like trial and error than proper problem solving. Usually this genre does have some type of internal logic either proper logic or “child logic”, (though admittedly most games have at least one extraordinarily silly solution), but Rufus is just mad… Often the solution is doing the most moronic thing possible intentionally.
And that leads us into the [b]cast[/b]. Rufus is a horrible protagonist, completely devoid of any charm, which usually saves other reckless and careless protagonists from coming off as horrible and selfish human beings. His lack of even the most basic human kindness and decency coupled with the attitude of self-importance and “I’m too cool for this place”, makes it damn near impossible to care about anything he does. Most of the rest of the characters are not much better, dull and forgettable, even if their designs make them somewhat physically interesting. I just couldn’t get invested in most of them, and ended up skipping a lot of dialogue, because a lot of it seemed pointless and when they didn’t interest me I just wanted to move it all along to get to where they might have me an item I needed or otherwise push me along in the puzzles.
[b]The story[/b] just doesn’t seem to fit. Saving the world, gathering friends and fighting against oppressors. Seriously? Someone who is this self-centered? How can it be that he gets friends, when he insults everyone he meets? [spoiler]Seriously he literally scratches his name into a girl’s electronic brain! And refused to clean it with a small delicate brush because that was beneath him. 
He murdered baby dolphins after being specifically told to leave them alone.
And he SHATTERED his girlfriend’s mind because he would rather have a lollipop than take the expensive material she needed for her brain surgery. DESPITE THE FACT THAT HE WASN’T THE ONE PAYING FOR IT! [/spoiler] It just really breaks any sort of immersion, even in a comedy game. Rufus isn’t a really an underdog hero type, like the story-arch seems to suggest. He is more a bumbling idiot, who falls from situation to situation without any awareness. I think he would fit such a story better, one where he is an accidental hero. Even if that is a bit of a cliché, having his enemies and maybe even the common people believe he is some sort of brilliant guy, rather than having (almost) everyone know he is a complete idiot. It kinda takes the punch out of a lot of jokes, when both we and the characters knows Rufus is going something stupid… again… and again… and again. I mean no one really gets surprised by it…


The comedy is more mixed… A bit of it works, the vast majority of it doesn’t. Which is in large parts due to the main character, and the context of the story. Many jokes rely on slapstick. While seeing Rufus get hurt the first time is satisfactory, it quickly loses its punch, because he hurts everyone around him too… And he is not a dignified character, seeing a clear loser being humiliated and hurt just isn’t that funny. Some jokes just aren’t really set up properly to be fun. [spoiler]Like the big masculine hairy guy turns out to have been soft and girly as a kid… But by then we had already seen Rufus walk all over him at multiple occasions. We had seen him with an explosive passionate girl, who almost killed him and who was clearly more in charge in their relationship. And he generally had a kind and gentle demeanor… So the joke didn’t really have any staying power, since he wasn’t the ideal macho man anyway.[/spoiler] Of course some of the jokes still work, and are amusing enough that you don’t give up on the game entirely. 

[u]Positives[/u]
There are two “characters” that I really enjoyed [b]Toni and Spunky Goal[/b]. [spoiler]Toni because she really mirrors my emotions towards Rufus. The horrible human-waste’s ex-girlfriend, she is tired of his freeloading behavior and shitty attitude and is a rather cynical lady, who clearly has a heart of fucking gold in there since she hasn’t kicked the bum out or killed him despite the horrible psychological torment he has put her and her loved ones through. I’d have loved for her to be a secondary playable protagonist to balance out Rufus, but sadly that wouldn’t fit the story. Still I enjoyed the brief moments with her. Spunky Goal, while just one of Goal’s personalities after Rufus shattered her mind for a lollipop, is the other character I truly enjoyed. Mostly because of the contrast between her and the actual Goal, who is more of a classic damsel in distress most of the time (and a pretty pathetic one at that, when you fall for a guy like Rufus), Spunky Goal however is a really fun contrast. An over the top tough girl, ready to beat your little boy butt for looking at her funny, inside the body of such a feminine little body. I appreciated her threatening Rufus.[/spoiler]
[b]The visuals[/b] I enjoyed the overall cartoony style of it, the background, the looks of the characters. I think that is one of the strong points of the game.
[b]The setting and world[/b] the setting is nice and simple, a planet that is overrun with junk all around, with the humans living there having adapted to the horrible environment, and an almost dreamlike city floating above their heads, which no one can get to. Simple, but with room for variations on the locations between the different games.

Welcome to Deponia, or as I like to call it, Modern Day Monkey Island.
It checks all the boxes in that regard.

Bumbling doofus for a protagonist, Check!

Daft slapstick comedy at every opportunity, Check!

Puzzles so frustrating and obscure you want to punch a hold through your monitor, Check!

All in the format of a classic third person point and click game. Proving the genre is still alive and well.

You follow the misadventures of Rufus, a self centred idiot who you will frequently want to punch in the face (and probably a lot more after you see all the things he does in the sewers of Deponia 3) as he tries to escape the junk-strewn planet of Deponia, accidentally uncovers a genocidal conspiracy and puts all his effort into "getting the girl" who is oh so subtly named Goal.

Needless to say, what follows is a bizarre adventure with memorable characters, hilarious dialogue and a strange platypus obsession.

What impresses me is the first game manages to wrap itself up nicely without being overly suggestive of a sequel. You rarely see that sort of thing in most AAA titles (*cough* *cough* Blazblue! *cough*) it's quite remarkable considering they actually planned it to be a trilogy back then according to the commentary. Though I couldn't bring myself to sit through it all so I turned it off. Sorry Poki.

Wow. Have I really spent 47 hours playing this game? Guess it's longer than I thought it was!

*cough* Anyway, by now you've probably heard some things about these games, about how the creators are the "German Lucasarts" [which seems a bit unfair given there isn't an American Lucasarts any more] and how the ending actually goes back in time and makes the game suck retroactively.

Well, I for one really enjoyed these games. There was a good balance between outright comedy and drama, the twists and turns of the plot keep you guessing right until the end, and there is actually some good character development. [With the exception of Cletus: I still don't know what that guy's after]. The design and animation is top-notch, and it seems to be impossible to get stuck or killed [with one exception, but you are warned several times!]

If I'd have just played the first game, I'd be a little more hesitant. I found Rufus to be a bit of a jerk and rather unlikeable, the backgrounds pretty though mostly static, and the puzzles largely illogical. Oh, and the game seemed to suffer from the same problem that Simon the Sorcerer did. It thinks it's funnier than it is.

However, these niggles are mostly fixed in the second and third games. Rufus actually undergoes some character development, and whilst he is largely out for himself, he does have a bit more compassion. The scenes are overflowing with little background events, birds [well, platypuses] flying, water ripping, flags blowing in the wind etc. The humour seems a litlte more restrained thanks to the intrusion of some well-placed drama [seriously - these games have some rather dark moments if you're not expecting them], and the puzzles.. well... it could just be that you need to adjust to their way of thinking but they started to make a lot more sense.

The creators do seem to have made point-and-click adventures their "thing", and rather than Telltale who seem to have rounded all the corners off and made their games simpler for a new generation, Deponia is aimed squarely at people who enjoyed these games when they were in their heyday. That doesn't mean they're old-fashioned though. The control interface is reasonably straight forward, the games are gorgeous (did I mention that?), the voice acting is excellent and the music is..well, it's alright. You can switch it off if it gets on your nerves.

As for the ending? Well, without meaning to spoil things too much, I can see why it's divisive, but I'm pleased that the developers didn't simply go for a "all the loose ends get tied up, the good guys live happily ever after and the bad guys get what they deserve" ending. Sure it's bittersweet, but why not? This game isn't for young children, you should be able to handle it.

I'm not going to compare the game to Monkey Island. Just because it's a point-and-click game doesn't mean it has to be like a Lucasarts game. It's not as wacky as Cokel's Gobliiins series, nor is it as serious as The Dig. Perhaps it's more like Sam and Max, with the gleefully anti-social protagonist. Regardless, if you like point-and-click games and want something with a good storyline and hours of gameplay, it's difficult to go wrong with this. And it is worth getting "The Complete" because besides giving you a discount, it also links the games together and gives you other bonus items as well. And it runs on Linux. Which is excellent.

I've played a lot 2D point and click games in the past, but this one was far the biggest I’ve encountered!

Even though this is a trilogy which is technically 3 games glued together, each of them had a lot going on and I do mean a LOT of interactions.

What makes it great is not only the amount of possible “right” choices but also wrong choices and combinations which triggered the voiced reply of your character for this specific choice you’ve made.  I must also mention the great amount of art and animated objects in every room, plus the animated scenes. Its things like these that make point and click games feel so alive and Deponia trilogy did its best at it.

I’ll be honest, I’m not really a fan, neither am I great at puzzles which frankly speaking, some of the combinations made very little if no sense at all, then again we’re playing as Rufus, one of the worst innocent human beings known to man. The game tries its best to make us hate him for every screwed up action he makes and that’s because well….it’s Rufus I guess, lol. Without him though there would be no wild adventure and….saving the world I guess, again.

The ending felt bitter sweet and anti-climactic, however this doesn’t ignore the fact that the rest of the game sucked, which it surely didn’t. [i] (Also there's Deponia Doomsday which continues after this trilogy). [/i] It’s overall worthy of being called a masterpiece!

Also I’m not completely sure guys, but I think the lead director likes minigames.
